thesis.problem: Image generation moved from research demo to production tool faster than the supply of models a company can actually build on. Most of the strongest systems are closed, reachable only through one vendor's API, which leaves a product team unable to run the model on its own infrastructure, inspect it, or fine-tune it for a house style.
thesis.solution: Black Forest Labs trains its own image and editing models, publishes open-weight versions alongside commercial ones, and sells the larger models to companies that want them inside their own products. The bet is that the open releases spread the toolchain and the enterprise versions pay for the research, with the founders' record on latent diffusion as the evidence they can keep pace.

thesis.problem: Large companies cannot see how their own processes actually run. An order-to-cash or purchase-to-pay flow touches ERP, CRM and supply-chain systems that each hold a fragment of the truth, so the duplicated payments, manual rework and stalled deliveries hiding inside them stay invisible to the people accountable for them.
thesis.solution: Celonis reconstructs the real path of every transaction from the event logs those systems already write, compares it against how the process was supposed to run, and quantifies the cost of each deviation. The product is sold to large enterprises as a platform that both diagnoses the gap and triggers the corrective action inside the underlying system.

thesis.problem: Restaurants still order from their suppliers by voicemail, fax and scribbled note, and a wholesaler's sales desk spends its morning transcribing those messages into an order system. Every transcription is a chance to send the wrong quantity, and the wrong quantity is food that gets thrown away.
thesis.solution: Choco gives the restaurant a messaging app for placing orders and the supplier a system that reads those orders straight into its own order processing, so the same instruction is only entered once. Selling to both sides of the same transaction is the point: the value only appears when the buyer and the seller are on the platform together.

thesis.problem: A large retailer's online shop is usually one monolithic platform that owns the product catalogue, the checkout, the pricing rules and the storefront design together. Changing anything customer-facing means a release of the whole system, which is why adding a new sales channel — an app, a kiosk, a marketplace listing — takes quarters rather than weeks.
thesis.solution: commercetools separates the commerce engine from the storefront and exposes it as APIs, so a retailer builds whatever front end it wants against the same catalogue, cart and order services. That is the 'headless' argument the company has made since before the term was common, and its customers are large enough that the flexibility is worth the integration work.

thesis.problem: Free machine translation is tuned for gist, not for text a company would put its name to. Businesses working across European languages either paid human translators for every contract, support reply and manual, or accepted output that read as translated — and most general-purpose engines would not let regulated firms keep the text off a third party's training data.
thesis.solution: DeepL trains its own translation and writing models rather than fine-tuning someone else's, and sells them to businesses as an API and as apps that plug into the tools staff already use. Enterprise contracts cover data handling and glossaries so that terminology stays consistent, and the same model line has been extended into writing assistance and spoken translation.

thesis.problem: Moving a container from a factory in Asia to a warehouse in Europe still runs on email, spreadsheets and phone calls between a shipper, a forwarder, a carrier and a customs broker. The company paying for the freight usually cannot say where its goods are, what the delay will cost, or which of its routes is quietly losing money.
thesis.solution: Forto acts as the freight forwarder itself and runs the booking, documents, customs and tracking on its own software, so the customer sees one live view of every shipment instead of reconstructing it from correspondence. Because the same platform records what each lane actually cost and how long it took, the data doubles as the basis for planning the next quarter's shipping.

thesis.problem: European armed forces run on hardware procured over decades, and the sensor data those platforms produce is largely unused at the speed a decision needs it. Buying capability through traditional prime contractors takes years, which leaves European and NATO forces reliant on American software for battlefield awareness.
thesis.solution: Helsing writes defence software rather than building the platforms it runs on: models that fuse feeds from cameras, radar and other sensors into a live picture of a battlespace, delivered as updatable software into existing aircraft, vehicles and drones. It funds its own research and sells directly to governments and to prime manufacturers as a partner, and has since extended into building strike drones and underwater systems of its own.

thesis.problem: In a mid-sized company, money leaves before finance knows about it. Employees pay on shared cards or their own, receipts arrive weeks later, and invoices are approved over email, so the finance team spends the month reconstructing what was spent rather than controlling it as it happens.
thesis.solution: Moss issues corporate cards with per-team budgets and approval rules, and pairs them with invoice capture and reimbursements in the same system, so every payment carries its receipt, cost centre and approver from the moment it is made. Entries flow into the accounting and ERP systems the company already runs, and the newer AI features are built to prepare work for sign-off rather than to act unsupervised.

thesis.problem: European law now makes a company answerable for things happening several tiers down its supply chain — forced labour at a subcontractor, deforestation behind a commodity, emissions it never measured. The evidence for those answers sits in purchasing systems, supplier questionnaires and site audits that were never built to be read together, so compliance becomes a rolling manual exercise repeated for every new regulation.
thesis.solution: osapiens runs one cloud platform on which each reporting duty is a separate module drawing on the same supplier and transaction data, so a company answers a new rule by switching on an application rather than starting a new project. The products are sold to large enterprises as compliance tooling, and the pitch is that the same data, once collected properly, also shows where a supply chain is slow or wasteful.

thesis.problem: Enterprise contact centres are expensive to staff and slow to scale, and the automation sold to them was built on rigid decision trees that break the moment a caller phrases something unexpectedly. Large brands that wanted to hand routine calls to software found it either failed the customer or could not be trusted to act on their systems.
thesis.solution: Parloa sells a platform for building, testing and supervising AI agents that hold spoken and written conversations and then carry out the resulting task in the company's own systems. The emphasis is on the management layer — simulation before deployment, guardrails and human sign-off — so that a large enterprise can run many agents across languages and channels under one set of controls.

thesis.solution: Personio packages the whole employee lifecycle — applicant tracking, onboarding, digital personnel files, absence, performance and payroll preparation — into one subscription that a company without a dedicated HR systems team can configure itself. thesis.problem: A great many small businesses sell one good product on Amazon and stall there, because the owner is also the buyer, the marketer and the logistics department. Individually they are too small to negotiate with factories or to fund the next product line; sold individually, they fetch a small-business price.
thesis.solution: Razor Group buys those sellers outright and runs them on shared systems for sourcing, pricing, advertising and supply chain, so the combined group has the volume to bargain with manufacturers and the data to decide what to make next. Growth has come as much from absorbing rival aggregators — Stryze, then the American company Perch — as from buying merchants.

disputed.note: A larger figure is widely attached to Razor: TechCrunch’s headline on the March 2024 Perch merger calls $1.7bn a valuation. Its article body measures something else — “the combined business has an enterprise value of $1.7 billion … with about $400 million of debt on its books”. Enterprise value counts that debt; a post-money equity valuation does not, and the post-money is what this register records. The $1.2bn here is Razor’s last stated post-money, struck at the April 2023 Series C and restated by TechCrunch at the time of the merger.

thesis.problem: Millions of employees in Germany, Italy and Spain are owed a tax refund and never claim it, because the return assumes vocabulary and paperwork most people do not have. The alternatives are a tax adviser whose fee can exceed the refund, or desktop software that still expects the user to know which boxes apply to them.

The company is deliberately aimed at simple tax situations — salaried people with a payslip — rather than at the complex cases advisers are built for.

thesis.problem: Retail investing in Europe was priced and packaged for people who already had money. Bank brokerage carried per-order commissions and custody fees large enough to make small, regular savings uneconomic, which left most Europeans dependent on state pensions they are unlikely to be able to live on.
thesis.solution: Trade Republic is a mobile broker with a full German banking licence: commission-free savings plans, fractional shares and ETFs, plus bonds, derivatives and crypto, with a flat external settlement fee instead of a percentage. It earns on order flow, interest on customer deposits and card interchange rather than trading commissions, and now operates across most of western Europe.

sources.title: Trade Republic strengthens its shareholder base in a €1.2 billion secondary round led by Founders Fund and other existing investors at €12.5 billion valuation.
sources.quote: Now, investors conducted a €1.2bn secondary transaction valuing the company at €12.5bn.

sources.title: Berlin’s Trade Republic nabs $900M led by Sequoia at a $5B+ valuation to take its neobroker app across Europe
sources.quote: Trade Republic, which lets people buy and sell shares, exchange-traded funds (ETFs), derivatives and (most recently) cryptocurrency by way of a mobile app that does not charge commissions (but does have a fee structure for various services), has raised $900 million in a Series C round of funding that values the Berlin startup at $5.3 billion, the startup confirmed.

sources.title: Trade Republic strengthens its shareholder base in a €1.2 billion secondary round led by Founders Fund and other existing investors at €12.5 billion valuation.
sources.quote: Trade Republic raised more than 1 billion euro in primary capital across its funding rounds and received a full banking license from the ECB in 2023.
